content: 1. Professor Ashraf Nabhan, from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Ain Shams University in Cairo, Egypt, contributed as a content expert and implementer for the guideline development. He declared no conflicts of interest. 2. Mari Nagai, Deputy Director and Health System Team Lead at the Bureau of International Health Cooperation, National Center for Global Health and Medicine in Tokyo, Japan, participated as a content expert and end-user. She declared no conflicts of interest. 3. Professor Hayfaa Wahabi, Chair of Evidence-Based Healthcare and Knowledge Translation at the College of Medicine, King Saud University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, contributed as a content expert and end-user. She declared no conflicts of interest. 4. Professor Dilys Walker, from the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Sciences at UCSF in San Francisco, USA, is the co-founder and president of PRONTO International, an NGO that designs and implements simulation and team training for obstetric and neonatal emergencies, including postpartum hemorrhage. She has donated funds to the organization. This conflict was not deemed significant enough to affect her participation in the guideline development group. 5. Professor Andrew Weeks, from the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom, served as a content expert and end-user. He is the chief investigator of the COPE trial and co-inventor of the Butterfly device for treating postpartum hemorrhage, both funded by NIHR research grants. This conflict was not considered serious enough to impact his participation. 6. The WHO recommendation on advance misoprostol distribution to pregnant women for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) was developed using a systematic evidence-based approach. The priority outcomes included maternal death, severe maternal morbidity, blood transfusion, and postpartum anemia, among others. 7. The evidence synthesis group reviewed data from two trials involving 570 women who had non-facility births. One trial was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study in Uganda, where women were randomized to receive either 600 mg of misoprostol or a placebo for self-administration after childbirth. The second trial was a stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial in Uganda, where women were given misoprostol for self-administration if they delivered outside a health facility or in facilities without oxytocin. 8. The Cochrane review included one study comparing advance misoprostol distribution to usual care for PPH prevention in non-facility births. The study reported on maternal mortality, blood transfusion, severe maternal morbidity, and side effects such as shivering, fever, and diarrhea. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low due to indirectness, few events, and small sample sizes. 9. Observational studies from countries such as Afghanistan, Ghana, India, Liberia, Nepal, and South Sudan suggest that advance misoprostol distribution increases uterotonic coverage for PPH prevention, with minimal reports of incorrect use or adverse events. These studies also indicate improved antenatal care attendance and facility births. 10. A quasi-randomized study in Afghanistan found that all women in the intervention areas used misoprostol correctly, and uterotonic coverage increased compared to control areas. However, outcomes related to blood loss and severe maternal morbidity were not reported.
